Worm self-propagation: burst of npm publish / git push from a single developer host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the propagation step the article quantifies as '73 repositories in under two minutes' on the Microsoft Azure orgs - a single dev host using a stolen npm/GitHub token to republish or push to many destinations in a tight window. Thresholds 5+ publishes or 10+ pushes in 10 minutes from one identity, excluding known CI hosts. Rationale: Article: 'spread across 73 repositories in under two minutes' on Microsoft Azure orgs and 'republishes infected versions of every package that token can publish'. A real developer rarely publishes 5+ npm packages or pushes to 10+ git remotes in 10 minutes; the worm fan-out is the differentiator. Threshold tuned to be sensitive enough to catch the Microsoft Azure-scale burst (~73 in 2min ≈ 36 actions/min) while staying above a maintainer's normal commit-and-push cadence. Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://perplexityaimagazine.com/ai-news/miasma-worm-microsoft-github-supply-chain-attack-2026/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/binding-gyp-supply-chain-attack-compromises-dozens-of-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1078.004 T1567
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Release engineer running `lerna publish` or `nx release publish` for a monorepo bulk release
  • Maintainer publishing a versioned set of related packages back-to-back
  • Developer rebasing a stack of branches and running `git push` for each
  • Git-flow style release where a feature-branch is pushed alongside main and a release tag
  • Bulk-rename or repo-migration tool legitimately pushing to many remotes
Suppression filter
| where not (SampleCmds has_any ("lerna publish","nx release","changeset publish","semantic-release"))  // legit monorepo bulk release tools
| where not (AccountName in~ ("release-eng","npm-publisher","github-actions[bot]"))  // known release identities
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full list of ProcessCommandLine in the 10-minute window - if they target distinct unrelated package names or unrelated org repos rather than a single monorepo, that's worm fan-out. Cross-reference the package names against the StepSecurity Miasma list (@vapi-ai/server-sdk, ai-sdk-ollama, jagreehal/*) and Hades list (ensmallen, embiggen, pyphetools, gpsea, ppkt2synergy). 2) Contain: revoke the npm token (`npm token revoke`), GitHub PAT, and any OIDC sessions for that user immediately. Force-yank affected versions via npm/PyPI security team contacts. Isolate the host. 3) Hunt: for each package the user just published, identify downstream npm consumers via DeviceFileEvents (npm install touching that package) over the last 24h - they're the next infection wave. Also pivot on UC1 to find the .vscode/.claude config files that landed before this burst.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm.cmd") and ProcessCommandLine has "publish")
   or  (FileName =~ "git.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "push" and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","--help")))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where DeviceName !startswith "ci-" and DeviceName !startswith "build-" and DeviceName !startswith "runner-" and DeviceName !startswith "gh-runner"
| summarize ActionCount = count(),
            DistinctCmds = dcount(ProcessCommandLine),
            SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', max(Timestamp), min(Timestamp))
            by DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where (FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm.cmd") and ActionCount >= 5)
     or (FileName =~ "git.exe" and ActionCount >= 10)
| order by ActionCount desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName has_any ("npm.exe","npm.cmd") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "publish")
   or  (ActingProcessName has "git.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "push" and not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","--help")))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where DvcHostname !startswith "ci-" and DvcHostname !startswith "build-" and DvcHostname !startswith "runner-"
| summarize ActionCount = count(),
            DistinctCmds = dcount(ActingProcessCommandLine),
            SampleCmds = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where (ActingProcessName has_any ("npm.exe","npm.cmd") and ActionCount >= 5)
     or (ActingProcessName has "git.exe" and ActionCount >= 10)
| order by ActionCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) AND @CommandLine:*publish*) OR (@Image:(*\\git.exe OR *\\Git.exe OR *\\GIT.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*push* AND -@CommandLine:*--dry-run*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ((ImageFileName=/\\npm(\.exe|\.cmd)$/i AND CommandLine=/publish/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\git\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/(?<!--dry-run.*)push/i))
| ComputerName!=/^(ci-|build-|runner-|gh-runner)/i
| bucket(span=10m, field=@timestamp, function=groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName], function=count(as=ActionCount)))
| ActionCount >= 5
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(Processes.process) as cmds values(Processes.process_path) as paths min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","npm.cmd") AND Processes.process="*publish*") OR (Processes.process_name="git.exe" AND Processes.process="*push*")) by host Processes.user Processes.process_name span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count >= 5 AND NOT match(user,"\$$") AND NOT match(host,"(?i)^(ci-|build-|runner-|agent-|gh-runner)")
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmds values(Processes.process_path) as paths min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","npm.cmd") AND Processes.process="*publish*") OR (Processes.process_name="git.exe" AND Processes.process="*push*")) by host Processes.user Processes.process_name span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count >= 5 AND NOT match(user,"\$$") AND NOT match(host,"(?i)^(ci-|build-|runner-|agent-|gh-runner)")
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/

            - '\powershell.exe'

            - 'DownloadString'

            - '-w hidden'

ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)

                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50751", "CVE-2026-50752")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50751", "CVE-2026-50752")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9d2da07aa6e7db3fbc36b36f0cfd74f78d5815f5ba55d0f0405cdd668bd13767", "7ca42f1f23dbdc9427c9f135815bb74708a7494ea78df1fbc0fc348ba2a161ae", "241a50befcf5c1aa6dab79664e2ba9cb373cc351cb9de9c3699fd2ecb2afab05", "522fdfaff44797b9180f36c654f77baf5cdeaab861bbf372ccfc1a5bd920d62e") or SHA1 in~ ("9d2da07aa6e7db3fbc36b36f0cfd74f78d5815f5ba55d0f0405cdd668bd13767", "7ca42f1f23dbdc9427c9f135815bb74708a7494ea78df1fbc0fc348ba2a161ae", "241a50befcf5c1aa6dab79664e2ba9cb373cc351cb9de9c3699fd2ecb2afab05", "522fdfaff44797b9180f36c654f77baf5cdeaab861bbf372ccfc1a5bd920d62e") or MD5 in~ ("9d2da07aa6e7db3fbc36b36f0cfd74f78d5815f5ba55d0f0405cdd668bd13767", "7ca42f1f23dbdc9427c9f135815bb74708a7494ea78df1fbc0fc348ba2a161ae", "241a50befcf5c1aa6dab79664e2ba9cb373cc351cb9de9c3699fd2ecb2afab05", "522fdfaff44797b9180f36c654f77baf5cdeaab861bbf372ccfc1a5bd920d62e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9d2da07aa6e7db3fbc36b36f0cfd74f78d5815f5ba55d0f0405cdd668bd13767", "7ca42f1f23dbdc9427c9f135815bb74708a7494ea78df1fbc0fc348ba2a161ae", "241a50befcf5c1aa6dab79664e2ba9cb373cc351cb9de9c3699fd2ecb2afab05", "522fdfaff44797b9180f36c654f77baf5cdeaab861bbf372ccfc1a5bd920d62e") or SHA1 in~ ("9d2da07aa6e7db3fbc36b36f0cfd74f78d5815f5ba55d0f0405cdd668bd13767", "7ca42f1f23dbdc9427c9f135815bb74708a7494ea78df1fbc0fc348ba2a161ae", "241a50befcf5c1aa6dab79664e2ba9cb373cc351cb9de9c3699fd2ecb2afab05", "522fdfaff44797b9180f36c654f77baf5cdeaab861bbf372ccfc1a5bd920d62e") or MD5 in~ ("9d2da07aa6e7db3fbc36b36f0cfd74f78d5815f5ba55d0f0405cdd668bd13767", "7ca42f1f23dbdc9427c9f135815bb74708a7494ea78df1fbc0fc348ba2a161ae", "241a50befcf5c1aa6dab79664e2ba9cb373cc351cb9de9c3699fd2ecb2afab05", "522fdfaff44797b9180f36c654f77baf5cdeaab861bbf372ccfc1a5bd920d62e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9d2da07aa6e7db3fbc36b36f0cfd74f78d5815f5ba55d0f0405cdd668bd13767", "7ca42f1f23dbdc9427c9f135815bb74708a7494ea78df1fbc0fc348ba2a161ae", "241a50befcf5c1aa6dab79664e2ba9cb373cc351cb9de9c3699fd2ecb2afab05", "522fdfaff44797b9180f36c654f77baf5cdeaab861bbf372ccfc1a5bd920d62e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — npm v12 delivers one of the biggest security improvements in years
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Node/npm parent spawning network or scripting child during package install · [LLM] Known malicious npm-supply-chain package SHA256 observed on disk or executed · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound to Shai-Hulud / npm-worm C2 (webhook.site, sfrclak.com, 142.11.206.73) from node/npm process tree · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TruffleHog secret-scanner binary execution on developer or CI endpoint · [LLM] Node/npm/bun process touching SSH, npm or GitHub credential files · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Node/npm parent spawning network or scripting child during package install AIInstallation Medium
Detects node/npm/yarn/pnpm processes spawning curl, wget, bun, powershell, mshta, cmd or sh — the postinstall/preinstall script execution chain abused by Nx s1ngularity, Shai-Hulud, axios hijack, and Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm campaigns to drop second-stage payloads on developer and CI machines. Rationale: Pivots on the exact behavioural chain the article calls out — `When anyone runs npm install, npm runs that script automatically as the user` followed by `downloads the real payload from an attacker server`. Anchors on node/npm/yarn/pnpm as parents and adds article-IOC strings (webhook.site, sfrclak.com, 142.11.206.73, bun.sh, trufflehog) for high-fidelity matches.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Native-module packages (node-gyp, sharp, canvas, bcrypt, node-sass) invoking curl/wget to fetch prebuilt binaries from GitHub during install
  • Playwright/Cypress/Puppeteer postinstall hooks downloading browser binaries
  • Husky/lefthook installing git hooks via shell child processes
  • Corporate-internal scaffolding tools (yo, create-react-app, nx) that legitimately call PowerShell during init
  • CI runners executing npm ci followed by helper scripts that shell out for asset downloads
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","playwright install","cypress install","puppeteer","electron","husky install") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("webhook.site","sfrclak.com","142.11.206.73","trufflehog"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent ProcessCommandLine — confirm it was an `install`/`ci` invocation, identify the package name from the cwd path (e.g. `node_modules\<pkg>`), and look up the package + version against npm registry and Aikido/Socket malware feeds. Check if the child made network connections to webhook.site/sfrclak.com/142.11.206.73. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, rotate any GitHub PAT, npm token, SSH key, AWS key and cloud session token stored in the user profile, force-revoke npm tokens via `npm token revoke`, and remove the package from node_modules + lockfile. 3) Hunt: pivot on the package name across all hosts that ran `npm install` against the same lockfile in the last 14d; query DeviceNetworkEvents for the same SHA256 contacting any of the IOC IPs/domains; check for new public GitHub repos created by the user's PAT.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","python.exe","python3.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","postinstall","preinstall","run-script"," ci ","npm exec","npx ") 
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("webhook.site","sfrclak.com","142.11.206.73","trufflehog","bun install","bun.sh","Invoke-WebRequest","Invoke-RestMethod","curl -fsSL","wget -q")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl","wget","bun","bash","sh")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","postinstall","preinstall","run-script"," ci ","npm exec","npx ")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("webhook.site","sfrclak.com","142.11.206.73","trufflehog","bun install","bun.sh","Invoke-WebRequest","Invoke-RestMethod","curl -fsSL","wget -q")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Suspicious Child Process Spawned by npm or Node During Install
id: 4f6c5a7e-8b9d-4a1c-9d0f-2a3b4c5d6e7f
description: Detects node, npm, yarn or pnpm spawning curl, wget, powershell, bun or other shell/scripting binaries during a package install — the postinstall lifecycle script execution chain used by Nx s1ngularity, Shai-Hulud and Mini Shai-Hulud npm worms.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall
author: SOC Detection Eng
date: 2026/06/11
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.cmd'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\npx.cmd'
      - '\yarn.cmd'
      - '\pnpm.cmd'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\bash.exe'
      - '\sh.exe'
  selection_context:
    - ParentCommandLine|contains:
        - ' install'
        - 'postinstall'
        - 'preinstall'
        - 'run-script'
    - CommandLine|contains:
        - 'webhook.site'
        - 'sfrclak.com'
        - '142.11.206.73'
        - 'bun install'
        - 'bun.sh'
        - 'trufflehog'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_context
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate native-module builds (node-gyp, sharp, canvas, bcrypt) downloading binaries via curl/wget
  - Postinstall scripts of dev tooling like husky or playwright fetching browsers
level: medium

Outbound to Shai-Hulud / npm-worm C2 (webhook.site, sfrclak.com, 142.11.206.73) from node/npm process tree AICommand & Control High
High-fidelity network detection for the article-specific C2 indicators — webhook.site, sfrclak.com and 142.11.206.73 — when the originating process is node/npm/yarn/pnpm/bun or a child spawned underneath them. Catches the first-stage beacon and credential exfiltration steps common to Nx s1ngularity, Shai-Hulud and Mini Shai-Hulud campaigns. Rationale: Anchors on three explicit article IOCs (142.11.206.73, sfrclak.com, webhook.site) and pins them to a node/npm process tree to eliminate the noise of webhook.site being used for general webhook testing. Article quote: `It fingerprints the machine, downloads the real payload from an attacker server, runs it`.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1567.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately testing a webhook.site URL via Node fetch/axios during integration work — distinguishable by ad-hoc REPL context vs install-time
  • QA/staging environments using webhook.site as a test sink for outbound webhooks
  • Internal SRE tooling that pipes test traffic through webhook.site to validate egress
  • Curl/wget invoked manually under a CI npm job for an unrelated artifact pull from one of these hosts (low likelihood)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "webhook-test" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\test\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent — confirm whether this fired inside an npm install lifecycle (parent cmdline contains `install`, `postinstall`, cwd is under `node_modules`). Capture the webhook.site path (often a unique UUID) and the package name. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress proxy/firewall, isolate the host, revoke any npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH credentials stored on the device or accessible to the user, and pull the malicious package version from any internal mirror. 3) Hunt: search the last 30d of DeviceNetworkEvents for the same RemoteIP/RemoteUrl across the estate, query EmailEvents for phishing targeting maintainers of any in-house packages, and check GitHub audit logs for new public repos or pushed branches with names like `shai-hulud` or `Shai-Hulud-Migration`.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "142.11.206.73"
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("webhook.site","sfrclak.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe","node","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, 
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "142.11.206.73"
   or DstHostname has_any ("webhook.site","sfrclak.com")
   or Url has_any ("webhook.site","sfrclak.com","142.11.206.73")
| extend SrcProcess = tostring(parse_json(tostring(EventOriginalUid)).process)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret-scanner binary execution on developer or CI endpoint AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution of the TruffleHog secret-scanner binary on developer/CI hosts — Shai-Hulud and Mini Shai-Hulud worms drop TruffleHog as the credential-harvest stage to scrape GitHub tokens, npm credentials, AWS keys and SSH keys before exfiltration. TruffleHog has almost no legitimate runtime use on developer endpoints outside dedicated security tooling. Rationale: Article explicitly names TruffleHog as the secret-scrape tool in Shai-Hulud: `ran TruffleHog to scrape secrets, and dumped them into public GitHub repos`. The binary name + canonical subcommand patterns (`trufflehog filesystem`, `trufflehog github`) are unique to this tool — extremely low false-positive surface outside known security-team usage.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised security/DevSecOps team running scheduled secret scans against internal repos — should be allowlisted by service-account name + host
  • Pre-commit hooks running trufflehog locally for developers who installed it themselves
  • GitHub Actions self-hosted runners executing trufflehog-actions on PR scanning
  • Internal CI pipelines piping trufflehog output to artifact storage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-secscan","svc-devsecops") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\security-tools\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent process and command line — confirm whether trufflehog was spawned by an npm install context (`node.exe` / `npm.cmd` ancestor) vs a known security-team service account. Identify the scan target from the cmdline. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke every credential reachable from the user's profile (GitHub PAT, npm token, AWS access keys, SSH keys, browser-stored secrets), and force-rotate them. Pull the originating npm package + version. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on POSTs from this host to webhook.site, sfrclak.com or 142.11.206.73; query GitHub audit logs for new public repos created by the impacted PAT within the next 24h (Shai-Hulud's exfil destination); look for the same trufflehog SHA256 across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("trufflehog.exe","trufflehog","trufflehog3.exe","trufflehog3","th.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("trufflehog filesystem","trufflehog github","trufflehog git --","trufflehog gitlab","trufflehog s3","trufflehog --only-verified")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcImage = FolderPath,
          ProcCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("trufflehog.exe","trufflehog","trufflehog3.exe","trufflehog3")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("trufflehog filesystem","trufflehog github","trufflehog git --","trufflehog gitlab","trufflehog s3","trufflehog --only-verified")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

tags:

Node/npm/bun process touching SSH, npm or GitHub credential files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects node/npm/bun and their child processes reading or writing under credential-bearing paths (~/.ssh, ~/.npmrc, ~/.config/gh, ~/.aws, ~/.docker, crypto wallet directories) — the discovery + credential-access behaviour every observed npm install-time worm performs after the initial postinstall script fires. Rationale: Targets the discovery/credential-access pattern called out by the kill-chain block: `the payload scans for tokens, SSH keys, and other goodies`. Pivots on the article-specific actor lineage — node/npm/bun reaching into ~/.ssh, ~/.npmrc, ~/.config/gh, wallet stores — which is anomalous outside the install of one or two specific tools.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1083 T1217
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm itself reading ~/.npmrc for registry auth during routine install — high-volume; needs allowlist of .npmrc-only access from npm.cmd parent
  • Yarn 2+ reading ~/.npmrc and ~/.yarnrc.yml for shared registry token
  • gh CLI extensions written in Node calling into ~/.config/gh
  • AWS SDK in Node app reading ~/.aws/credentials at process startup (long-running services, not install-time)
  • Crypto wallet dev tooling (Hardhat, Truffle) legitimately reading Ethereum keystore directories during local testing
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "npm.cmd" and FileName =~ ".npmrc" and ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified") and tostring(FolderPath) endswith @"\")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("yarn install","yarn add","yarn config") and FileName == ".npmrc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent chain — is this `npm.cmd → node.exe` during install (suspicious) or `node.exe` as a long-running app process (likely benign). Pull the cwd to identify the calling package and check whether the user-account session shows a fresh `npm install`/`npm ci`/`yarn install` in the last 30 minutes. 2) Contain: if install-context confirmed, isolate the host, force-rotate every credential type read (SSH, npm, GitHub PAT, AWS, crypto-wallet seeds), and remove the package + version from node_modules and lockfile. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256 of the InitiatingProcessParentFile across the estate; query DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to webhook.site/sfrclak.com/142.11.206.73 from the same host within ±10 min; check GitHub audit log for the user's PAT being used from new IPs in the next 24h.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe","node","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.config\gh\", @"\.docker\config.json", @"\AppData\Roaming\npm\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Solana\", @"\AppData\Local\Yarn\")
   or FileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa",".npmrc","credentials","config.json","hosts.json","wallet.dat")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules\\.bin\\eslint"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe","node","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.config\gh\", @"\.docker\config.json", @"\AppData\Roaming\npm\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Solana\")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa",".npmrc","credentials","wallet.dat")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known malicious npm-supply-chain package SHA256 observed on disk or executed AIInstallation Medium
IOC-driven detection for the eight SHA256 file hashes tied to the Nx s1ngularity / Shai-Hulud / axios hijack / Mini Shai-Hulud malicious package corpus. Hits indicate the host pulled a compromised version into node_modules or executed the dropped payload. Rationale: Direct SHA256 / SHA1 hash IOCs supplied alongside the article — the highest-fidelity signal available. Each hit indicates the host pulled or executed a known-malicious package version from Nx s1ngularity / Shai-Hulud / axios / Mini Shai-Hulud. No behavioural inference required.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal malware sandbox or detonation host intentionally fetching the package for analysis — should be allowlisted by hostname/group
  • DFIR analyst manually downloading the indicator file to a forensic workstation for triage
  • Vulnerability-scanning tooling caching indicator files for signature testing
  • Threat-intel platform agent (Tines/Anomali/Recorded Future) syncing IOC bundles to disk — pair filter excludes their service-account paths
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FolderPath of the hit — confirm it is under `node_modules\<pkg>`, identify the exact package + version, and look up the package against npm registry. Cross-reference the host's `package-lock.json` and CI history. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke and rotate every credential reachable from the user's profile (npm token via `npm token revoke`, GitHub PAT, AWS access keys, SSH keys, browser-stored secrets, crypto wallet seeds), and purge the package from the project + lockfile. Search for and revoke any new public GitHub repos created by the affected PAT. 3) Hunt: query last 60d of DeviceFileEvents for the same SHA256 across every host; pivot DeviceNetworkEvents to look for the same host beaconing webhook.site/sfrclak.com/142.11.206.73; query GitHub audit logs for the impacted user account showing publish-token use against unrelated packages (lateral worm spread).

Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process Actions on Objectives High
Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore.json, MetaMask, Exodus, Atomic, Phantom data.
ATT&CKT1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Bitcoin\", @"\Exodus\", @"\Electrum\wallets\", @"\MetaMask\", @"\Phantom\", @"\Atomic\Local Storage\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Bitcoin\",
                                  @"\Exodus\", @"\Electrum\wallets\",
                                  @"\MetaMask\", @"\Phantom\",
                                  @"\Atomic\Local Storage\")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe",
                                  "electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable meta-ads-mcp installation inventory (CVE-2026-48039) on managed hosts · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 (CVE-2026-48039 exploitation)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-48039: Meta Ads MCP: Unauthenticated HTTP MCP Tool Ex
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Meta Graph API outbound request carrying access_token in URL query string
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 (CVE-2026-48039 exploitation) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to the meta-ads-mcp /mcp endpoint that arrive with no Authorization header on the default TCP 8080 listener. Per CVE-2026-48039, AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch() at http_auth_integration.py:272 does not return 401 and forwards the request to downstream MCP tool handlers, so any 200 OK response to an unauthenticated POST /mcp is the exploitation signature. Rationale: Article explicitly names default port 8080, the /mcp HTTP endpoint, and the AuthInjectionMiddleware bypass that returns HTTP 200 instead of 401 when no Authorization header is present. The combination of POST + /mcp + 8080 + 200 OK + missing Authorization header is the literal exploitation footprint, not a generic pattern. Cross-checked GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr advisory page. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal CI/CD or test harness calling /mcp without auth during local-dev smoke tests against the Docker image
  • Load balancer or service-mesh health-check probes hitting /mcp with no Authorization header
  • Legitimate clients that authenticate via pipeboard_token header (named in the codepath) rather than Authorization — these may also lack Authorization but should not be unauthenticated externally
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, internal Tenable) probing /mcp as part of CVE-2026-48039 verification
  • Reverse-proxy retries that strip headers on internal hops
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr startswith "10." or SrcIpAddr startswith "192.168." or SrcIpAddr matches regex "^172\\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\\.") and not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","GoogleHC","Tenable","Nessus","Qualys"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the SrcIpAddr / RemoteIP of the request and identify the MCP host (DvcHostname); confirm the host is running meta-ads-mcp ≤ 1.0.108 (`pip show meta-ads-mcp`). Check whether subsequent /mcp calls from the same source IP succeeded and which tool names were invoked (e.g., get_ad_accounts). Step 2 — Contain: Block the source IP at the perimeter, take the meta-ads-mcp container offline or restrict the listener to 127.0.0.1, and immediately rotate the META_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable in Meta Business Manager. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot to UC2 to see if the token already leaked outbound (graph.facebook.com URLs containing access_token=). Audit Meta Ads activity log for ad-account reads/writes from unfamiliar source IPs or user-agents over the prior 30 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8080
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn","node.exe","docker.exe","com.docker.backend.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "meta-ads-mcp"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "meta_ads_mcp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/mcp"
| where DstPortNumber == 8080 or HttpHostName has "8080"
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) or HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization == ""
| where HttpStatusCode startswith "2"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DvcHostname, DstPortNumber, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

@http.method:POST (@http.url:*\/mcp* OR @http.url_details.path:*\/mcp* OR @http.url_details.path:*\/MCP*) (@network.client.port:8080 OR @http.host:*:8080) @http.status_code:[200 TO 299] -@http.useragent:*kube-probe* -@http.useragent:*ELB-HealthChecker*
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 LocalPort=8080 ConnectionDirection=1
| ContextImageFileName=/(python|python3|uvicorn|gunicorn|node|docker)\.exe?$/i OR ContextImageFileName=/meta[_-]ads[_-]mcp/i

Meta Graph API outbound request carrying access_token in URL query string AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound HTTPS requests to graph.facebook.com where the URL query string contains the access_token= parameter. Per CVE-2026-48039 the vulnerable meta_ads_mcp api.py:136 appends the operator token to the URL as a query parameter — proper Meta SDK usage sends it via Authorization: Bearer header, so any access_token= in a URL targeting graph.facebook.com is a direct indicator of the vulnerable code path (and also exposes the long-lived token in proxy logs, browser histories, and any TLS-terminating middleboxes). Rationale: The article shows the literal vulnerable URL pattern (`https://graph.facebook.com/v24.0/me/adaccounts?...&access_token=FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789`) and points to api.py:136 (`request_params["access_token"] = access_token`) and the remediation that recommends moving the token to an Authorization header. Detecting `access_token=` in a graph.facebook.com URL is therefore both a vulnerability indicator AND a credential-leak indicator regardless of whether exploitation actually occurred. Cross-checked against the Meta Graph API v24.0 documentation which recommends Authorization header usage. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://developers.facebook.com/docs/graph-api/overview/authentication
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1041
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy/internally-built Meta SDK clients that intentionally include access_token in URL — still worth flagging as a credential-hygiene finding even when not malicious
  • Developer browser testing against the Graph API explorer where the explorer copies token to the URL
  • Proxy log re-ingestion of historical requests after a token rotation (already-rotated token reappears in old logs)
  • Mobile/SDK clients on older Facebook SDK versions that pre-date Bearer-token migration
  • Other vulnerable MCP servers in the org following the same pattern (true positives, not FPs — escalate)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("graph_api_explorer.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "debug_token"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Extract the access_token value from the URL (8-char preview only; treat full value as credential material), decode against Meta debug_token endpoint to identify the app_id and user_id that owns it, and check the source host — is it a known meta-ads-mcp deployment? Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revoke the token via Meta Business Manager (Settings → Business Integrations → revoke), purge it from proxy logs and SIEM raw store per credential-handling policy, and patch or take offline the source meta-ads-mcp instance. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot to UC1 to check whether the same MCP host received unauthenticated /mcp POSTs (confirms exploitation rather than internal misuse). Audit graph.facebook.com activity from arbitrary external IPs using the leaked token; look at Meta Ads change history for ad account writes during the exposure window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "graph.facebook.com"
| where RemoteUrl has "access_token="
| extend TokenPreview = strcat(substring(extract(@"access_token=([^&\"\s]+)", 1, RemoteUrl), 0, 8), "...")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, TokenPreview
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(
  ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DstHostname endswith "graph.facebook.com" or HttpHostName endswith "graph.facebook.com" or Url has "graph.facebook.com"
  | where Url contains "access_token="
  | extend TokenPreview = strcat(substring(extract(@"access_token=([^&\"\s]+)", 1, Url), 0, 8), "...")
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, TokenPreview
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DestinationHostName endswith "graph.facebook.com" or RequestURL has "graph.facebook.com"
  | where RequestURL contains "access_token="
  | extend TokenPreview = strcat(substring(extract(@"access_token=([^&\"\s]+)", 1, RequestURL), 0, 8), "...")
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SrcHostname, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, TokenPreview
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable meta-ads-mcp installation inventory (CVE-2026-48039) on managed hosts AIReconnaissance High
Asset-discovery hunt that surfaces any Defender-managed host running pip:meta-ads-mcp at a version covered by CVE-2026-48039 (≤ 1.0.108). Useful for closing the AuthInjectionMiddleware exposure proactively rather than waiting for the exploitation telemetry in UC1/UC2. Rationale: Article names the affected package (`pip:meta-ads-mcp`) and the affected version range (≤ 1.0.108) explicitly; the CVE is registered as CVE-2026-48039. Using Defender TVM CveId lookup avoids guessing about Python module paths and surfaces both Windows and Linux hosts. The process-event fallback catches hosts where the package isn't yet indexed by TVM but the daemon is running. Cross-checked the GHSA advisory tracking ID. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched hosts running 1.0.109+ that briefly appeared in TVM during a delayed inventory sync
  • Test hosts intentionally running the vulnerable version in an air-gapped lab for security research
  • Hosts where the Python process is bound to 127.0.0.1 only (not exploitable network-wide, lower priority but still worth patching)
  • Container scanners or vulnerability-management tools instantiating a meta-ads-mcp container to verify the CVE
  • Stale TVM data from decommissioned hosts that still report meta-ads-mcp installed
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: For each hit, confirm the meta-ads-mcp version with `pip show meta-ads-mcp` or container image digest; identify the listener — `ss -tlnp | grep 8080` (Linux) or `netstat -ano | findstr :8080` (Windows) — and whether it binds 0.0.0.0 (exploitable) or 127.0.0.1 (low risk). Step 2 — Contain: For network-reachable instances, restrict 8080 to localhost via firewall, upgrade to a confirmed-patched version (≥ 1.0.109 once tagged), and rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN immediately as a precaution. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot to UC1 to check whether the host received any unauthenticated /mcp POSTs from the Internet during its exposure window. Pivot to UC2 to confirm no token already egressed via graph.facebook.com URL leakage. Document remaining instances in the vulnerability tracker.

Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the three hard-coded GitHub commit-search query strings the Miasma supply-chain worm uses as its three independent C2 channels (PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, Python payload delivery). These strings have zero legitimate business presence and are the highest-fidelity Miasma indicator available. Rationale: The three strings 'DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom', 'TheBeautifulSandsOfTime' and 'firedalazer' are the hard-coded GitHub commit-search queries each Miasma C2 channel uses (PAT discovery, JS payload, Python payload). They are confirmed by SafeDep's analysis, BleepingComputer's report, and a parallel TheHackerNews write-up. Zero legitimate business processes contain these tokens. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-supply-chain-attack-compromises.html • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst running these strings through their own grep/search tooling for hunting
  • SOC engineer pasting the IOCs into a script or note file
  • Security researcher cloning or reading SafeDep / Cloudsmith write-ups in a developer IDE that logs URL paths
  • Sandbox / detonation environment intentionally executing a Miasma sample for analysis
  • Automation that ingests OSS-supply-chain advisories and writes IOCs to a database column
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe") and not (FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\","\\detonation\\","\\analyst-tools\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process that emitted the string is not an analyst hunting tool, a CTI ingestion script, or a known sandbox. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain; if the string was in a network URL, identify what process issued the GET against api.github.com/search/commits. 2) Contain: if the originating process is a node/python/git/curl invocation on a developer machine or CI runner, isolate the host from network, revoke any GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems publish tokens and JFrog Artifactory credentials owned by that user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same three strings org-wide; pivot on the parent process and SHA256 to find sibling executions; review the developer's git push history for npm/PyPI/RubyGems package versions published in the last 7d for unexpected new releases or postinstall scripts.
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256, Source = strcat("Net:", RemoteUrl);
union ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
union From4688, FromAsim
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma Worm GitHub Commit Search C2 Magic Strings
id: a7d4e8b2-9c3f-4e1d-b8a5-7f2e9d8c4a1b
description: Detects command-line invocations containing the three GitHub commit-search C2 query strings used by the Miasma supply-chain worm (variant of Shai-Hulud) for PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, and Python payload delivery.
references:
  - https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-supply-chain-attack-compromises.html

author: Detection Engineering

(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 OR #event_simpleName=SyntheticProcessRollup2 OR #event_simpleName=ScriptControlScanInfo)
| CommandLine=/(DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom|TheBeautifulSandsOfTime|firedalazer)/i OR ScriptContent=/(DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom|TheBeautifulSandsOfTime|firedalazer)/i

ENDPOINT

Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts for git clone / npm install / pip install / curl / wget operations that reference the briefly-public 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' GitHub repositories which leaked the worm's source on 2026-06-08. A match means the host has either ingested the leaked toolkit or is being staged with it. Rationale: 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' is the exact repository slug SafeDep and BleepingComputer report appeared on GitHub from 2026-06-08 hosting the leaked toolkit. The string is uniquely tied to Miasma and would only surface in dev-tool command lines or proxy URLs when a host is cloning, installing or downloading the leaked source. Cross-checked via SafeDep, BleepingComputer and TheRegister. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1105 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel team intentionally cloning the leaked repo into a sandbox for analysis
  • Security researcher fetching the source on a developer workstation for write-up
  • SOAR / TIP ingesting OSS advisory feeds and storing the repo URL as an IOC string
  • Vulnerability scanner or SCA tool fingerprinting against known-malicious repo names
  • Blue-team CTF or training environment seeding the toolkit deliberately
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\") and FolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process that issued the clone/install/fetch — confirm it is not a sanctioned analyst sandbox or CTI ingestion job. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and any subsequent npm/pip postinstall script execution from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node/python child processes spawned within 1 hour of the clone, revoke GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems/Artifactory publish tokens belonging to the user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the three Miasma C2 commit-search strings (see related UC) on the same host and across the org; review the user's recent package publishes for unexpected versions; check GitHub Actions workflows in any repo they touched for newly-added steps referencing untrusted secrets or external scripts.
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let DevTools = dynamic(["git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (DevTools) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevTools)
    | where ProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Network";
union isfuzzy=true ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or TargetProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
let FromProxy = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL contains MiasmaRepo or DestinationHostName contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, Account = SourceUserName, NewProcessName = "", CommandLine = RequestURL, ParentProcessName = "", Source = "Proxy";
union From4688, FromAsim, FromProxy
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc
