Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Defender TVM flags CVE-2026-48063 (vulnerable Baileys npm package) on host AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts where Defender Threat & Vulnerability Management has identified the npm:baileys / npm:@whiskeysockets/baileys package at a vulnerable version (< 6.7.22 or 7.0.0-rc.1 ≤ x < 7.0.0-rc12). This is the cleanest, lowest-FP route to find exposed WhatsApp-bot/automation hosts before exploitation via a crafted protocolMessage payload. Rationale: Direct CVE pivot — the advisory itself supplies CVE-2026-48063 as the canonical identifier. TVM/SBOM-grounded detection is the lowest-FP shape for a pure library vulnerability with no host-side TTPs. No external corroboration needed; the GitHub Security Advisory IS the authoritative source.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerability_Management.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Stale TVM data shortly after a successful upgrade (next TVM scan will clear it)
  • Dev/test workstations where baileys is installed but never connected to a real WhatsApp session
  • TVM version-parsing miss-attributing a back-ported security fix in a forked baileys build
  • Container build images flagged but never deployed to runtime
  • Pre-release ≥7.0.0-rc12 incorrectly version-compared by the scanner
Suppression filter
| where VulnerabilitySeverityLevel in ("High","Critical")
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "7.0.0-rc12" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "7.0.0-rc.12"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SoftwareVersion sits in the vulnerable range (< 6.7.22, or 7.0.0-rc.1 ≤ x < 7.0.0-rc12). Identify the package owner via repo, code-owner file, or LoggedOnUsers. Check if the host actually has a live WhatsApp session (look for sustained TCP to *.whatsapp.net / web.whatsapp.com from node.exe). 2) Contain: open a P2 patch ticket for owner to upgrade to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12. Workaround until patched — drop messages.upsert events containing a requestId field and set shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false in socket config. 3) Hunt: enumerate every other host with the file-event UC (paired UC2) to find shadow-IT baileys deployments TVM missed; pivot on parent node.exe command lines referencing automation scripts.

| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-48063"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, LoggedOnUsers
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-48063"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, OSPlatform, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, LoggedOnUsers
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Baileys npm package install/presence on Windows endpoints AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for file-write activity inside node_modules\baileys or node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys directories — surfaces hosts running the vulnerable WhatsApp library even when TVM/SBOM tooling has no signal on the npm package. Pair with UC1 (TVM) to cover environments without SBOM ingestion. Rationale: Uses the exact package paths from the advisory's affected-packages list (npm:baileys and npm:@whiskeysockets/baileys). File-path hunting catches shadow-IT installs that TVM/SBOM never enrolled. Cross-platform path variants (\ vs /) included for WSL/dev containers. Excludes Defender self-scan noise.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate corporate WhatsApp bot/automation projects running an already-patched baileys version (≥6.7.22 or ≥7.0.0-rc12)
  • Developer workstations where engineers clone open-source baileys for unrelated work
  • Jenkins/GitHub Actions self-hosted runners pulling baileys as a build-stage transitive dependency
  • Container build hosts producing baileys-containing images that are deployed elsewhere
  • Backup/restore agents replaying historical node_modules archives onto recovery hosts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\AppData\Local\Temp\", "\Windows\Temp\") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsiExec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the actual baileys version from the host's package.json (DeviceFileEvents won't tell you the version, only the path). If owner cannot be identified from the directory tree, use InitiatingProcessAccountName / LoggedOnUsers from DeviceInfo. 2) Contain: if vulnerable version (< 6.7.22 or 7.0.0-rc.1 ≤ x < 7.0.0-rc12), open a patch ticket and apply the workaround (drop messages.upsert events containing requestId, set shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false). For internet-facing bot hosts treat as priority. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for outbound traffic to *.whatsapp.net / web.whatsapp.com from node.exe to confirm an active WhatsApp session is bound to the vulnerable lib; enumerate other repos in the same project group that may share the dependency.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\", "/node_modules/baileys/", "/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), FileCount = count(), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 25), Installers = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\baileys\", @"\node_modules\@whiskeysockets\baileys\", "/node_modules/baileys/", "/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), FileCount = count(), SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 25), Installers = make_set(ActingProcessName, 10)
          by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Vulnerable Baileys npm package present on host (CVE-2026-48063)

Installation of Aikido-flagged malicious npm packages on developer endpoints AIDelivery High
Detects npm/yarn/pnpm installs resolving to the specific package@version combinations called out in the article — axios 0.30.4 / 1.14.1, postmark-mcp 1.0.16-1.0.18, plain-crypto-js 4.2.1, @bitwarden/cli 2026.4.0. Catches the supply-chain ingress before postinstall fires. Rationale: Pivots on the exact package@version strings the article names (axios 0.30.4/1.14.1, postmark-mcp 1.0.16-1.0.18, plain-crypto-js 4.2.1, @bitwarden/cli 2026.4.0). Article body + kill-chain Phase 1 IOCs.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-team red-team or threat-emulation install of the IOC packages for testing
  • Internal repro of the Aikido advisory by an engineer on a sandbox laptop
  • CI build cache of a research VM that retained the package in node_modules
  • Renovate/Dependabot scanning workflow surfacing the version in dry-run mode
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("sandbox-runner.exe","redteam-vm.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the device + developer; pull the full command line and parent (was this an AI-agent automation in Slack/CI, or a manual install?). Check whether node_modules already contains the package. 2. Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response, revoke any npm/cloud/SSH/GitHub tokens reachable from the device's home directory, rotate Bitwarden master password if @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 was pulled. 3. Hunt: cross-reference Slack audit logs for an AI-bot-approved PR in the prior hour; look across the fleet for the same IOC packages in DeviceFileEvents writes to package-lock.json/yarn.lock.

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (BadSpecs) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (BadSpecs)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

npm postinstall hook spawning a shell interpreter on a developer device AIInstallation High
Catches the article's exact execution chain: node/npm running a postinstall/preinstall script that immediately spawns cmd, PowerShell, bash, sh, or wscript/cscript/mshta — the textbook supply-chain payload pattern flagged by the Aikido advisory. Rationale: Targets the article's literal execution narrative: 'pulls a new dependency, executes the postinstall hook' — node/npm as the spawner, shell as the child. Parent-cmdline filter pins it to install-hook context, not interactive node use. Kill-chain Phase 2 detection hint.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / node-pre-gyp native module compile scripts (legitimate cmd.exe / sh.exe spawn during install of e.g. bcrypt, sharp)
  • Electron / Playwright postinstall downloading browser binaries with curl
  • Husky git-hook installer spawning a shell during `npm install`
  • Lerna / nx monorepo install orchestrators running cross-package scripts
  • Yarn berry's `node-modules` linker reorganising .bin shims
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","node-pre-gyp","prebuild-install","husky","playwright install","electron install","puppeteer")) and not (FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\bcrypt\\" or FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\sharp\\")
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the full parent + child command lines and the package whose postinstall fired (resolve from node_modules path); is this a known native-build module (node-gyp/sharp/bcrypt) or an unknown package? 2. Contain: isolate the host, terminate the descendent chain, suspend the developer's npm publish token and any GitHub PATs scoped to the device. 3. Hunt: pivot on the package name across the fleet via DeviceFileEvents writes to node_modules; check DeviceNetworkEvents from the host in the 5 minutes after the shell spawned for the article's C2 IPs/domains; check Slack audit logs for an AI-agent-approved PR that pulled the dependency.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","install.js","install.cjs","node_modules\\.bin")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
  ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
  ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
  ChildImage  = FolderPath,
  ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
  SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","install.js","install.cjs","node_modules")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm Postinstall Hook Spawning a Shell Interpreter
id: a1f2c3d4-5e6f-47a8-9b1c-2d3e4f5a6b7c
description: Detects node/npm/yarn/pnpm spawning cmd, PowerShell, bash, sh, wscript, cscript, mshta, curl, or certutil during a postinstall/preinstall hook on a developer workstation.

Execution of binaries matching Aikido article SHA1 hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hard-IOC sweep for the three SHA1 hashes (2553649f..., d6f3f62f..., 07d889e2...) tied by Aikido Intel to the GlassWorm / TeamPCP / postmark-mcp postinstall payloads. Triggers on either process execution or file landing. Rationale: Three SHA1 hashes are explicit hard IOCs published alongside the article — zero-FP signal when matched. Kill-chain Phase 2 explicitly lists these hashes. Worth a 90-day retrospective sweep on first deploy.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher re-analysing the IOCs in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel team detonating the sample in an isolated detonation VM
  • Incident-response retained artifact already known-quarantined by Defender
  • EDR vendor's own validation hash test on a security-team device
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the hit isn't from a known security-research sandbox or AV vendor test machine; pull file path, signer, parent process. 2. Contain: isolate the host immediately, take a memory image before reboot, revoke all secrets reachable from the developer's home directory (AWS, npm, GitHub PATs, kubeconfig, Bitwarden vault), force-rotate the developer's SSO password and reset MFA. 3. Hunt: pivot on the parent npm package name fleet-wide; check the kill-chain C2 IPs/domains in DeviceNetworkEvents from the host going back 90 days; review GitHub audit log for the developer's PAT for bulk-clone activity.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="Process"),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="File")
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1, Source="Process"),
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where TargetFileSHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName=ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1=TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileName, Source="File")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Developer-host beacon to GlassWorm / TeamPCP C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control High
Outbound network or DNS from any endpoint to the four C2 IPs (142.11.206.73, 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255) or the two domains (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) named in the article. Highest priority when the initiating process is node/npm/Code.exe. Rationale: Six hard network IOCs (4 IPs + 2 domains) from kill-chain Phase 6 — direct match against the Aikido article's C2 list. Enrichment flag on node.exe / Code.exe / browser process owner identifies the developer-device pivot the article calls out.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel ingestion job pre-fetching the IOCs for sandboxing
  • Web filter / proxy testing the IOC list with active probes
  • Researcher visiting giftshop.club via a controlled browser
  • Defender ASR test traffic
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("misp-feed.exe","otx-fetcher.exe","threatfox-sync.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "TI-SANDBOX-"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source device, the initiating process tree, and whether the traffic was blocked at proxy/firewall vs allowed. 2. Contain: isolate the device via EDR, sinkhole the domains at the recursive resolver, block the IPs at egress, force-revoke all secrets reachable from the developer's home directory (AWS, npm, GitHub PATs, Bitwarden, kubeconfig). 3. Hunt: retro-sweep 90 days of DeviceNetworkEvents and DNS across the fleet for the same IOCs; cross-reference with kill-chain Phase 1 IOC package installs on the same hosts in the prior 24h.
let BadIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (BadIPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (BadDomains)
| extend Suspect_NodeOrIDE = InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","Code.exe","electron.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Suspect_NodeOrIDE
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
union
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Src=SrcHostname, SrcUser=SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol, Source="Network"),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (BadDomains)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Src=SrcHostname, SrcUser=SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname=tostring(DnsResponseName), DstPortNumber=int(null), Url=tostring(DnsQuery), AppProto="dns", Source="DNS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Beacon to GlassWorm / TeamPCP C2 Infrastructure
id: c4d5e6f7-8a9b-4c0d-1e2f-3a4b5c6d7e8f
description: Detects outbound connections or DNS queries from any endpoint to the C2 IPs and domains published in the Aikido June 2026 advisory.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

  product: windows
detection:

      - '142.11.206.73'
      - '45.32.150.251'

      - '70.34.242.255'

    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'giftshop.club'

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:(142.11.206.73 OR 45.32.150.251 OR 45.32.151.157 OR 70.34.242.255) OR @DestinationHostname:(*giftshop.club* OR *sfrclak.com*))) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:(*giftshop.club* OR *sfrclak.com*))
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemoteAddressIP4="142.11.206.73" OR RemoteAddressIP4="45.32.150.251" OR RemoteAddressIP4="45.32.151.157" OR RemoteAddressIP4="70.34.242.255"))
OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/giftshop\.club|sfrclak\.com/i)

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255") OR All_Traffic.dest IN ("giftshop.club","sfrclak.com") OR All_Traffic.url="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Traffic.url="*sfrclak.com*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_user All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Postinstall-driven read of cloud credentials and SSH keys from developer home AIActions on Objectives Medium
A node/npm-spawned process reading ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.npmrc, ~/.kube/config or a Bitwarden vault file — the credential-theft step the article describes ('cloud credentials, SSH keys, npm publish tokens, Kubernetes configs'). Rationale: Pairs the article's named credential stores (cloud creds, SSH keys, npm tokens, kubeconfig) with node.exe parent — high-signal because legitimate node code rarely reads ~/.aws/credentials or ~/.ssh/id_* during a postinstall. Kill-chain Phase 4 detection hint.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • aws-sdk-js / aws-vault helper modules legitimately reading ~/.aws/credentials at runtime
  • ssh2 / simple-git npm modules reading ~/.ssh/id_rsa for repo auth during a build
  • kubectl-node wrapper modules reading ~/.kube/config
  • Bitwarden CLI legitimate authenticated session refresh
  • Developer running `npm login` writes .npmrc
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws-sdk","aws-vault","@kubernetes/client-node","simple-git","node-ssh","ssh2")) and not (FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\@aws-sdk\\")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the npm package whose postinstall touched the credential file (walk the InitiatingProcessParentId chain) — is the package on the Aikido IOC list? 2. Contain: rotate every credential that lived in the touched files (AWS keys, SSH keys + replace authorized_keys, npm publish tokens, kubeconfig tokens, Bitwarden master password); isolate the host; pull memory before reboot. 3. Hunt: check CloudTrail / Azure AD / GitHub audit logs for use of those credentials from any IP not previously seen for the developer's identity in the prior 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
   or ActionType has "Open"
| where (FolderPath has_any (@"\.aws\credentials", @"\.aws\config", @"\.ssh\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.kube\config", @"Bitwarden\data.json", @"@bitwarden\")
     or FileName in~ ("credentials","id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa",".npmrc","kubeconfig","data.json",".env"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","Code.exe","electron.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","node_modules","install.js")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
  InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
  InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.ssh/","/.npmrc","/.kube/config","Bitwarden\\data.json","@bitwarden")

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

China-Linked JDY Botnet Expands to 1,500+ Devices for Cyber Reconnaissance

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have warned of a "resurgence and expansion" of JDY, a covert network associated with China-nexus state-sponsored threat actors. "The JDY botnet comprises over 1,500 SOHO [small office and home office] and IoT devices and operates as a centrally controlled, high-performance scanner used to discover, fingerprint, and continuously map exposed services at scale," Lumen's

CVEsCVE-2026-35616
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1528

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] JDY-style reconnaissance — internal host high-fanout mixed-protocol scanning · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] JDY Linux shell dropper — architecture-aware MIPS/MIPSEL payload retrieval
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] JDY botnet self-delete — Linux ELF executes then unlinks its own image · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
JDY Linux shell dropper — architecture-aware MIPS/MIPSEL payload retrieval AIInstallation High
Hunts for the JDY first-stage shell dropper behavior on Linux SOHO/IoT/edge hosts: a curl/wget/tftp invocation that pulls a payload whose URL or filename embeds one of the architecture tokens (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) the dropper uses to select the right binary. Highly article-specific because the dropper enumerates exactly this set. Rationale: Anchors on the exact architecture-token set the article calls out (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) inside a download tool's cmdline — a combination that doesn't appear in benign sysadmin/package-manager activity. Corroborated against Lumen Black Lotus Labs' KV-botnet writeup (same MIPS-router targeting) and BleepingComputer's reporting on the JDY expansion. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/kv-botnet-dont-call-it-a-comeback/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/ • https://blog.lumen.com/routers-roasting-on-an-open-firewall-the-kv-botnet-investigation/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OpenWrt/DD-WRT firmware update scripts pulling MIPS images by architecture name
  • Embedded-systems developers cross-compiling/downloading test binaries for MIPS targets onto Linux jump hosts
  • Yocto/Buildroot CI workers fetching MIPS toolchains over HTTP
  • Network appliance vendor maintenance scripts that name-tag firmware by architecture
  • Researchers/reverse-engineers downloading public malware samples for analysis from MalwareBazaar/VX-Underground
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("apt","apt-get","dpkg","yum","dnf","opkg","pacman","zypper","snap")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("apt","unattended-upgrades","buildroot","yocto")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pull the parent process tree — confirm whether the curl/wget was launched by a legitimate package manager (apt/yum/opkg) or by an interactive shell / cron / unknown parent. Resolve the destination URL and check it against Black Lotus Labs' JDY IOC list on GitHub. Step 2 (Contain): If the host is a SOHO router, embedded device, or production server with no MIPS-development purpose, isolate from the network and snapshot for forensics — the binary self-deletes so capture /proc/<pid>/exe before kill. Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on the destination IP/host across DeviceNetworkEvents (or ImNetworkSession) for the last 30 days to find sibling infections. Check for downstream high-fanout scanning from the host (UC #3).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","ftpget","tftp","busybox")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)\b"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","://",".onion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","ftpget","tftp","busybox")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)\b"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","://",".onion")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JDY Botnet Linux Dropper - MIPS Architecture Payload Fetch
id: 8b5a4d1c-3f72-4e89-9b14-2e7c5f8a1d36
description: Detects the JDY botnet first-stage shell dropper retrieving an architecture-specific payload (mips/mipsel/mips64/mipsel64) via curl/wget/tftp/busybox on Linux SOHO/IoT hosts.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-to-1500.html
  - https://blog.lumen.com/kv-botnet-dont-call-it-a-comeback/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/ftpget'
      - '/tftp'
      - '/busybox'
  selection_arch:
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)\b(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)\b'
  selection_url:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'http://'
      - 'https://'
      - '.onion'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_arch and selection_url
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:(curl OR wget OR ftpget OR tftp OR busybox)) @process.command_line:(*mips* OR *mipsel* OR *mips64* OR *mipsel64*) @process.command_line:(*http\:\/\/* OR *https\:\/\/* OR *.onion*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 #event_platform=Lin
| ImageFileName=/(curl|wget|ftpget|tftp|busybox)$/i
| regex("(?i)\\b(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)\\b", field=CommandLine)
| regex("https?:\\/\\/|\\.onion", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

JDY botnet self-delete — Linux ELF executes then unlinks its own image AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the JDY post-execution defense-evasion behavior described in the article: the scanner binary is launched then deleted from disk so a live process has no on-disk backing file. Correlates a process-create on a non-system path with a delete of that same path within seconds. Rationale: The article explicitly states 'Once the malware is launched, it's deleted from disk' — a distinctive evasion the article calls out as a JDY characteristic. By joining process-create with same-path file-delete within a tight window, we surface this specific behavior on Linux hosts that ship Defender/ASIM telemetry without alerting on package-manager temp-file churn (filtered via the FP block). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/kv-botnet-dont-call-it-a-comeback/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Self-extracting installer shell archives (.run, makeself) in /tmp that extract → exec → cleanup
  • Ansible/Salt/Chef one-shot runners that drop a script in /tmp, execute, then remove
  • snapd / flatpak sandbox helpers in /var/run that are short-lived
  • CI runner ephemeral build steps inside /tmp/buildXXX
  • pip/npm post-install hooks that compile and clean up in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where ParentName !in~ ("sh","bash","dash") or true
| where not (ImagePath has_any ("/tmp/ansible-","/tmp/saltrun-","/tmp/build","/tmp/pip-","/tmp/npm-","/var/run/snapd/","/run/user/"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): For the matched process, dump /proc/<pid>/exe and /proc/<pid>/maps before the process exits — the deleted ELF is still mapped and can be recovered from memory. Capture the SHA256 and check against JDY samples on Black Lotus Labs' GitHub IOC repo. Step 2 (Contain): If recovered binary matches JDY tooling (or shows raw-socket SYN-scan code paths), isolate the host. Block any C2 IPs the live process is talking to (DeviceNetworkEvents → RemoteIP for that ProcessId). Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on the parent process — JDY's dropper is a shell script; the parent should be /bin/sh or /bin/bash. Find the dropper invocation across the fleet and check for the architecture-specific payload pattern (UC #1).
let WindowSec = 30;
let ExecEvents = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/run/","/run/")
    | project ExecTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName,
              ImagePath = FolderPath, ImageName = FileName,
              SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, ParentName = InitiatingProcessFileName;
let DeleteEvents = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed")
    | where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/run/","/run/")
    | project DelTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DelPath = FolderPath, DelName = FileName,
              DelInitiator = InitiatingProcessFileName;
ExecEvents
| join kind=inner DeleteEvents on DeviceId
| where ImagePath == DelPath and ImageName == DelName
| extend GapSec = datetime_diff('second', DelTime, ExecTime)
| where GapSec between (0 .. WindowSec)
| project ExecTime, DelTime, GapSec, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ImagePath, ImageName, SHA256, ParentName, DelInitiator, ProcessCommandLine
| order by ExecTime desc
let WindowSec = 30;
let ExecEvents = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/run/","/run/")
    | project ExecTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ImagePath = ActingProcessName, CmdLine = ActingProcessCommandLine,
              Hash;
let DeleteEvents = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventType == "FileDeleted"
    | where TargetFilePath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/run/","/run/")
    | project DelTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DelPath = TargetFilePath;
ExecEvents
| join kind=inner DeleteEvents on DvcHostname
| where ImagePath == DelPath
| extend GapSec = datetime_diff('second', DelTime, ExecTime)
| where GapSec between (0 .. WindowSec)
| project ExecTime, DelTime, GapSec, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ImagePath, Hash, CmdLine
| order by ExecTime desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(EXECVE OR DELETE) @process.executable.path:(*/tmp/* OR */var/tmp/* OR */dev/shm/* OR */var/run/* OR */run/*) -@process.executable.path:*/snap/* -@process.executable.path:*/.cache/yarn/*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 #event_platform=Lin ImageFileName=/^\/(tmp|var\/tmp|dev\/shm|var\/run|run)\//
| rename(field=ImageFileName, as=ExecPath)
| join({#event_simpleName=FileDeleted #event_platform=Lin TargetFileName=/^\/(tmp|var\/tmp|dev\/shm|var\/run|run)\//}, field=aid, key=aid, include=[TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, _time], mode=inner)
| ExecPath = TargetFileName
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ExecPath], function=[count(), min(_time)])

JDY-style reconnaissance — internal host high-fanout mixed-protocol scanning AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single internal host (likely a compromised SOHO/IoT device or jump box recruited into JDY) exhibiting the article's hallmark scanning shape: high-volume, simultaneous TCP/TLS/UDP/ICMP probing against many distinct external destinations in a short window. Tuned to fire on the rate + protocol-diversity + destination-fanout combination, which is the JDY tasking signature. Rationale: Article calls out the exact scanning shape: 'high-volume TCP, SSL, UDP, and ICMP-assisted probing' on the same node. Detecting that protocol mix combined with a fanout floor (200+ destinations, 20+ ports, <5 conn/dst mean) is far more article-specific than a generic 'noisy source' alert and is the JDY tasking signature. Corroborated against Lumen's KV-botnet writeup which describes identical mixed-protocol probing from the predecessor cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/kv-botnet-dont-call-it-a-comeback/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/ • https://blog.lumen.com/routers-roasting-on-an-open-firewall-the-kv-botnet-investigation/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046 T1584.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7 InsightVM/Tenable.io scan engines)
  • Internet measurement projects (Censys/Shodan-like scanners) running on a security research host
  • RUM/synthetic monitoring agents (Datadog, NewRelic) hitting many endpoints
  • MDM/EDR agents doing bulk policy refresh against many cloud endpoints
  • P2P clients on user laptops (BitTorrent DHT chatter looks similar)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("nessus-scanner-01","qualys-engine-01","rapid7-engine-01")
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("scanner","probe","monitor"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify the source DeviceName/SrcIpAddr — is it on the asset inventory? If yes, is it a sanctioned scanner (Nessus engine, internal probe)? Check OS/role: SOHO/IoT firmware, network appliance, IP camera, NVR are high-suspicion. Step 2 (Contain): If unsanctioned, network-isolate via NAC or 802.1X quarantine VLAN. For an IoT/SOHO device, power-cycle is rarely sufficient — JDY survives reboot per Lumen; pull the device and reimage. Step 3 (Hunt): Look for the dropper chain on this host (UC #1) and for outbound connections to Tor entry nodes from the same source. Pull DNS for the past 7 days from the host's resolver — JDY uses Tor relays as C2, so look for .onion lookups or known Tor consensus IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionFailed","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize 
    DistinctDsts = dcount(RemoteIP),
    DistinctPorts = dcount(RemotePort),
    DistinctProtos = dcount(Protocol),
    Protos = make_set(Protocol, 10),
    SamplePorts = make_set(RemotePort, 20),
    TotalConns = count()
    by DeviceName, DeviceId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctDsts >= 200 and DistinctProtos >= 3 and DistinctPorts >= 20
| extend MeanConnsPerDst = TotalConns * 1.0 / DistinctDsts
| where MeanConnsPerDst < 5     // scanner shape: many destinations, few packets each
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr) and DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.16."
| summarize 
    DistinctDsts = dcount(DstIpAddr),
    DistinctPorts = dcount(DstPortNumber),
    DistinctProtos = dcount(NetworkProtocol),
    Protos = make_set(NetworkProtocol, 10),
    TotalConns = count()
    by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctDsts >= 200 and DistinctProtos >= 3 and DistinctPorts >= 20
| extend MeanConnsPerDst = TotalConns * 1.0 / DistinctDsts
| where MeanConnsPerDst < 5
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:* -@DestinationIp:(10.* OR 192.168.* OR 172.16.* OR 172.17.* OR 172.18.* OR 172.19.* OR 172.20.* OR 172.21.* OR 172.22.* OR 172.23.* OR 172.24.* OR 172.25.* OR 172.26.* OR 172.27.* OR 172.28.* OR 172.29.* OR 172.30.* OR 172.31.*)
#event_simpleName=/^NetworkConnectIP[46]$/
| ConnectionDirection=0 OR ConnectionDirection=1
| !cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | !cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | !cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)

| DistinctDsts >= 200

| order by conn_count desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1). Ivanti Sentry handleMessage endpoint exploitation (CVE-2026-10520) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry MICS endpoint /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage, which watchTowr Labs identified as the unauthenticated RCE sink reaching the backend handleExecute() in CVE-2026-10520 (CVSS 10.0). Pre-patch, ANY hit on this endpoint from the internet (or from an unexpected internal source) is a candidate exploitation attempt; post-patch, hits should redirect to the login page so successful POSTs with 2xx are anomalous. Rationale: watchTowr Labs explicitly named /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage as the vulnerable endpoint reaching handleExecute() — this is a unique, non-generic path string that exists nowhere else legitimate on a Sentry appliance and produces near-zero baseline noise. The path is on the Sentry box itself so the gold telemetry is WAF/proxy logs (CommonSecurityLog/Datadog web sources), with the Defender query catching lateral exploitation attempts.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanning (Tenable Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7 InsightVM, watchTowr ASM) probing the endpoint post-disclosure to confirm patch status
  • Internal red-team / purple-team exercises against the new CVE
  • Ivanti TAC support sessions where legitimate admin troubleshooting reaches the endpoint via VPN
  • Pre-prod / staging Sentry appliances being validated against pentest tooling
  • Synthetic monitoring scripts written by the platform team to verify the patch's redirect-to-login behavior
Suppression filter
// In Sentinel — exclude known scanner source IPs (maintain a Watchlist 'VulnScanners') and Ivanti support ASNs
| where SourceIP !in (toscalar(_GetWatchlist('VulnScanners') | summarize make_set(SourceIP)))
| where tostring(RequestClientApplication) !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "InsightVM", "Nuclei", "watchTowr")
Response runbook
Step 1 — TRIAGE: Identify the source IP and confirm it is unauthenticated (no prior valid session cookie / Authorization header on requests from the same SourceIP within 1 hour). Pull the full POST body from the WAF log to look for shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `$(`, backticks). Check whether the Sentry appliance is patched to R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1. Step 2 — CONTAIN: If unpatched and the request returned 2xx, block the source IP at the perimeter and isolate the Sentry appliance from the management network. Force expire all Sentry admin sessions and rotate any credentials/certificates the appliance brokers (MDM enrollment certs, SCEP, CA). Step 3 — HUNT: Pivot on the Sentry appliance's outbound connections in the 24h before/after the request — look for new reverse shells, cron jobs, or SSH keys on the appliance. Cross-check CVE-2026-10523 (auth bypass) for any newly-created admin accounts in the Sentry admin portal. Review MDM-managed device fleet for unauthorized profile pushes
// Catches lateral-pivot exploitation attempts where an internal endpoint hits the Sentry MICS endpoint.
// Inbound-from-internet exploitation must be caught via the Sentinel/WAF query — Sentry appliance does not ship to Defender.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
   or AdditionalFields has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
// Primary surface: WAF / proxy / firewall logs forwarded as CEF.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
| extend SuccessfulPost = (RequestMethod =~ "POST" and tostring(EventOutcome) startswith "2")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName,
          DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, EventOutcome,
          RequestClientApplication, Activity, SuccessfulPost
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Ivanti Sentry MICS handleMessage Endpoint Access (CVE-2026-10520)
id: 6f4e2b50-2d4a-4c2f-9bca-1c0c7c4f5f02
description: Detects HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage endpoint, the unauthenticated RCE sink in CVE-2026-10520 reaching the backend handleExecute() component. Post-patch, requests should be redirected to the login page; any successful POST is highly suspicious.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ivanti-fortinet-and-sap-release-patches.html
  - https://forums.ivanti.com (Ivanti Sentry advisory)
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - cve.2026.10520
logsource:
  category: webserver
level: high
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage'
  selection_post:
    cs-method: 'POST'
  condition: selection and selection_post
falsepositives:
  - Authorized vulnerability scans (Tenable / Qualys / Rapid7) post-disclosure
  - Ivanti support tooling during legitimate troubleshooting
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:cloudflare OR source:fortinet OR source:paloalto) (@http.url:*/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage* OR @url:*/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage* OR @http.url_details.path:*/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage*) @http.method:POST
# log group: /aws/wafv2/<your-acl> (or ALB access logs if Sentry sits behind AWS)

| filter httpRequest.uri like /\/mics\/api\/v2\/sentry\/mics-config\/handleMessage/
| filter httpRequest.httpMethod = "POST"
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

Vulnerable Ivanti / Fortinet / SAP versions exposed to June 2026 critical CVEs AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt across Defender TVM (and Sentinel's mirror of the same table) for assets running versions of Ivanti Sentry, FortiSandbox, SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP/Java, SAP Commerce Cloud, or SAP Data Hub that are vulnerable to the seven critical CVEs disclosed June 10 2026. Output is a prioritized patch worklist — these are the assets that will be exploited next if any of these CVEs get weaponized. Rationale: Article enumerates the exact affected versions (FortiSandbox 5.0.0–5.0.5 / 4.4.0–4.4.8, Ivanti Sentry pre-R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1) and all seven CVE IDs. Defender TVM is the authoritative source for what's running where — this turns the patch advisory into an actionable worklist. Prioritization in the query reflects the CVSS hierarchy with CVE-2026-10520 (10.0, unauth RCE) at the top.
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lag: assets patched in the last 24h still appearing as vulnerable until next scan cycle completes
  • Decommissioned / retired appliances still in TVM inventory (filter by Heartbeat / last-seen)
  • Non-production lab Sentry/SAP/FortiSandbox instances intentionally left unpatched for security testing
  • Vendor-managed appliances where the customer cannot apply patches directly (contact vendor instead)
Suppression filter
// Suppress retired / non-reporting devices
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(2d) | distinct DeviceId) on DeviceId
// Suppress lab tag if you label TVM with MachineGroup
| where MachineGroup !contains "lab" and MachineGroup !contains "sandbox-test"
Response runbook
Step 1 — TRIAGE: Sort the output by Priority then IsInternetFacing=true; the internet-facing P0 assets (CVE-2026-10520 unpatched Ivanti Sentry) are the queue. Cross-reference each PublicIP against attack-surface management to confirm exposure. Step 2 — CONTAIN: For internet-facing Ivanti Sentry on vulnerable versions, place a temporary WAF rule blocking POST to /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage until R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1 is applied; coordinate emergency change windows with the MDM team. For FortiSandbox, restrict WEB UI access to management VLAN only pending 5.0.6 / 4.4.9 upgrade. Step 3 — HUNT: Once patched, run UC1 retroactively over the prior 90 days against the Sentry asset IPs to look for pre-disclosure exploitation. For SAP NetWeaver, additionally pull SAP Security Audit Log entries for RFC errors (CVE-2026-27671 telltale) and unusual SAML assertions (CVE-2026-44748).
let TargetCves = dynamic(["CVE-2026-25089","CVE-2026-10520","CVE-2026-10523","CVE-2026-44748","CVE-2026-27671","CVE-2026-22732","CVE-2026-40128"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in (TargetCves)
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| extend Priority = case(
    CveId == "CVE-2026-10520", "P0 — unauth RCE 10.0",
    CveId in ("CVE-2026-10523","CVE-2026-44748"), "P1 — auth bypass / SAML wrapping",
    CveId == "CVE-2026-27671", "P1 — unauth memory corruption",
    "P2")
| project Priority, DeviceName, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, OSPlatform,
          SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, RecommendedSecurityUpdateId
| order by Priority asc, IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

| project Priority, DeviceName, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName,

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
